extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for what makes a composition a poem and the signs of poetic genius — including formal, imagistic, musical, intellectual, and imaginative qualities. Focuses on how parts should relate, what marks originality, and practical symptoms of poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a poem (immediate object: pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is that species of composition which is opposed to works of science by proposing for its immediate object pleasure, not truth; and from all other species (having pleasure in common) it is discriminated by proposing to itself such delight from the whole as is compatible with a distinct gratification from each component part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition emphasizes purpose (pleasure over truth) and a structural demand: every component part should yield distinct gratification. The author notes that poetry may exist without metre but that whatever is called a poem must produce a harmonious whole whose parts justify attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance of parts with metrical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: If metre be superadded, all other parts must be made consonant with it; they must be such as to justify the perpetual and distinct attention to each part which an exact correspondent recurrence of accent and sound are calculated to excite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When metre or rhyme is present it imposes obligations: diction, imagery, and arrangement must harmonize with metric demands. Mere addition of metre to prose-like material is insufficient; metre should be organically integrated and justified by the material and arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and mutual support of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate poem must be one the parts of which mutually support and explain each other; all in their proportion harmonizing with, and supporting the purpose and known influences of metrical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid two anti-patterns: (1) a series of striking lines or distiches each absorbing attention and becoming separate wholes; (2) an unsustained composition whose parts do not attract or support the general result. The ideal is interdependence of parts producing a single harmonious effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasurable activity of mind / the 'journey' principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader is carried forward, not merely or chiefly by the mechanical impulse of curiosity, but by the pleasurable activity of mind excited by the attractions of the journey itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem should make the process of reading enjoyable in its own right — pauses, retrogressions, returns and progressive attractions should stimulate and sustain attention rather than merely aiming at a final solution or point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry demands more continuous and equal attention than prose
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of poetry is the exciting of a more continuous and equal attention than the language of prose aims at, whether colloquial or written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer poetic compositions must select and arrange material so the non-poetic parts remain 'in keeping' with the poetic quality; poetry's arrangement is an artful selection designed to sustain this heightened attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as synthetic/harmonizing power
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's Imagination is the power that blends and reconciles opposites: sameness with difference; the general with the concrete; the idea with the image; the individual with the representative; novelty with the familiar; order with deep emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is described as the soul of poetic genius: it synthesizes discordant qualities, subordinating art to nature and manner to matter, thereby transforming material into a unified poetic whole. This balancing of opposites is a key test of poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical sense / sweetness of versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect sweetness of versification; its adaptation to the subject; and the power displayed in varying the march of the words without passing into a loftier and more majestic rhythm than was demanded by the thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sense of musical delight (a 'music in the soul') and skill in versification indicate imagination and genuine poetic promise. Richness and sweetness of sound, if original rather than imitative, are highly favorable signs in a young poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and pictorial vividness (picturesque power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic picture-word makes the object so sensuous to us that we are more conscious of the object than of the words; the poet 'seizes the very type of a thing' and presents it vividly and permanently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective pictorial imagery can be more than translatable into a material painting; it makes impressions clear and immediate. Examples (Dante, Shakespeare) are cited as models. This ability is prized but must be subordinated to larger unity and passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery must be modified by predominant passion / unity of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Images, however beautiful, become proofs of original genius only as far as they are modified by a predominant passion; by associated thoughts or images awakened by that passion; by reducing multitude to unity or succession to an instant; or when a human and intellectual life is transferred to them from the poet's spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely picturesque lines may belong equally to topography or tour descriptions; to be genuinely poetic, imagery must be integrated with feeling and thought so that it contributes to a dominant, unified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of subject remote from personal circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark of genius is the choice of subjects very remote from the private interests and circumstances of the writer himself; subjects taken immediately from the author's personal sensations are often equivocal proofs of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects drawn solely from personal experience may indicate technical skill but can be a fallacious pledge of original poetic power. Genuine poetic instinct often treats larger, less self-referential themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought (philosophic magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth and energy of thought: no man was ever yet a great poet without being at the same time a profound philosopher. Poetry is the blossom and the fragrancy of all human knowledge, thought, passion, and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual force must accompany sensory and imagistic gifts. Great poetry combines creative power with intellectual energy — knowledge, meditation, and comprehension are necessary to sustain lasting poetic greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs acquired trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery, affecting incidents, just thoughts, and the art of their combination may be acquired as a trade by a man of talent and much reading; but the sense of musical delight and the power of reducing multitude into unity are gifts of Imagination and cannot be learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between cultivated technique (which a diligent writer can acquire) and inborn imaginative gifts. Technical facility without imaginative synthesis yields only transient or second-rate poetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic justification / organic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can permanently please which does not contain in itself the reason why it is so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic features (diction, meter, imagery) must be organically necessary to the work. Ornament or form that lacks an internal reason or necessity will not give durable pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intention as classificatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction (what a writer calls a poem) is at least competent to characterize the writer's intention; if a man chooses to call every composition a poem because it is rhyme or measure, most leave his opinion uncontroverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While intention matters for classification, the critic still applies substantive standards (unity, musicality, imagination) to judge legitimacy. The label alone does not exempt a work from these criteria.
